statement: Let $K$ be a field and let $G \le \mathrm{GL}_n(K)$ be a [finitely generated](c:finitely-generated-group) [linear group](c:linear-group). Then $G$ has a [solvable](c:solvable-group) subgroup of finite index, or $G$ contains a nonabelian [free group](c:free-group).

hypotheses.text: $G$ is a subgroup of $\mathrm{GL}_n(K)$, so $G$ is a [linear group](c:linear-group).

conclusion: Either some [solvable](c:solvable-group) subgroup of finite index lies in $G$, or $G$ contains a nonabelian [free group](c:free-group).

proofs.name: Proximal elements and ping-pong
proofs.slogan: Reduce to a Zariski dense subgroup of a semisimple group, find proximal elements over a local field, and play ping-pong with their powers.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem for any field $K$. The solvable case is the case where the Zariski closure has a solvable identity component. The proof is an outline of Tits's argument.

roles.why: The field supplies absolute values and the algebraic-group structure used in all steps.
Matrices let the Zariski closure and its [solvable](c:solvable-group) radical be formed.
Finite generation makes the coefficient field finitely generated and gives an unbounded place.

steps.slogan: Reduce to a Zariski dense subgroup of a connected semisimple group.
steps.detail: Let $H$ be the Zariski closure of $G$ and let $H^0$ be its identity component. If $H^0$ is [solvable](c:solvable-group), then $G \cap H^0$ is a solvable subgroup of finite index and the proof ends. Otherwise divide $G \cap H^0$ by the solvable radical to get a group $\bar G$, Zariski dense in a semisimple group.

steps.slogan: Embed the coefficient field in a local field where the image is unbounded.
steps.detail: The matrix entries of the generators generate a finitely generated field. An infinite finitely generated linear group is unbounded for some absolute value of this field. So the field embeds in a local field $k$ (real, complex, $p$-adic or Laurent series) for which $\bar G$ is not relatively compact.

steps.slogan: Find an element that acts proximally on projective space.
steps.detail: Tits builds, from a suitable irreducible representation over $k$, an element $\gamma \in \bar G$ with one eigenvalue of strictly largest absolute value. Such an element has an attracting point and a repelling hyperplane in projective space.

steps.slogan: Move the fixed data of two proximal elements into general position.
steps.detail: Zariski density gives $g \in \bar G$ such that $\gamma$ and $g\gamma g^{-1}$ have attracting points and repelling hyperplanes in general position. Each attracting point then lies outside both repelling hyperplanes.

steps.slogan: Apply the ping-pong lemma to large powers of the two elements.
steps.detail: For large $N$, the maps $\gamma^N$ and $(g\gamma g^{-1})^N$ send the complement of small neighborhoods of their repelling hyperplanes into small disjoint neighborhoods of their attracting points. The ping-pong lemma then shows that they generate a free group of rank 2.

steps.slogan: Lift the free subgroup to $G$ and combine both cases.
steps.detail: A [free group](c:free-group) is projective, so a free subgroup of $\bar G$ lifts to a free subgroup of $G$ through the surjection onto $\bar G$. So $G$ contains a nonabelian free subgroup unless $H^0$ is solvable, and then $G$ is virtually solvable.

concepts.c:solvable-group: Solvability of the closure is the first alternative of the theorem.
concepts.c:free-group: Ping-pong produces the free subgroup of rank 2.
concepts.c:linear-group: The group is a group of matrices over a field.
concepts.c:finitely-generated-group: Finite generation gives a finitely generated field and an unbounded place.

source.ref: J. Tits, Free subgroups in linear groups, Journal of Algebra 20 (1972), 250-270
source.note: The steps outline Tits's proof; Tits proves the proximal-element and general-position steps in his sections on semisimple groups over local fields.

statement: Let $F(t_0, t_1, \dots)$ be the generating function of the [intersection numbers](c:intersection-number) of $\psi$-classes on the [moduli spaces of stable curves](c:moduli-space-of-curves) $\overline{\mathcal M}_{g,n}$. Then $e^{F}$ is a [tau function](c:tau-function) of the [KdV hierarchy](c:kdv-hierarchy), and $U = \partial^2 F/\partial t_0^2$ solves $\partial_{t_1}U = U\,\partial_{t_0}U + \tfrac{1}{12}\partial_{t_0}^3 U$.

hypotheses.text: $F = \sum_{g,n} \frac{1}{n!} \sum_{d_1,\dots,d_n} \langle \tau_{d_1}\cdots\tau_{d_n}\rangle_g\, t_{d_1}\cdots t_{d_n}$ collects the [intersection numbers](c:intersection-number) with $2g-2+n>0$ and $\sum d_i = 3g-3+n$.

conclusion: The function $U = \partial^2F/\partial t_0^2$ satisfies the KdV equation $\partial_{t_1}U = U\,\partial_{t_0}U + \tfrac{1}{12}\partial_{t_0}^3 U$, and $e^{F}$ satisfies the whole KdV hierarchy.

proofs.name: Kontsevich's matrix Airy function
proofs.slogan: Write the intersection numbers as a sum over ribbon graphs, match it with the matrix Airy integral, and read KdV from its determinant formula.
proofs.scope: The whole statement (Kontsevich's theorem, called the Witten conjecture). The proof is an outline of Kontsevich's argument; Mirzakhani later gave another proof by Weil-Petersson volumes.

roles.why: The generating function is the object that the graph sum and the matrix integral compute.

steps.slogan: Express the intersection numbers as integrals over the space of metric ribbon graphs.
steps.detail: Strebel differentials identify $\mathcal M_{g,n} \times \mathbb R_{>0}^n$ with the space of metric [ribbon graphs](c:ribbon-graph) of genus $g$ with $n$ faces. Under this identification, the classes $\psi_i$ become explicit combinatorial 2-forms built from the face perimeters.

steps.slogan: Write the generating function as a sum over trivalent ribbon graphs.
steps.detail: Integrating over the edge lengths gives a sum over trivalent ribbon graphs. The sum has terms $\prod_e 2/(\lambda_{i(e)}+\lambda_{j(e)})$ divided by the order of the automorphism group. It equals $\sum \langle\tau_{d_1}\cdots\tau_{d_n}\rangle \prod_i (2d_i-1)!!\,\lambda_i^{-2d_i-1}$.

steps.slogan: Identify the graph sum with the matrix Airy integral.
steps.detail: The graph sum is the Feynman expansion of the Hermitian matrix integral $\int e^{\,i\,\mathrm{tr}(X^3)/6}\, e^{-\mathrm{tr}(\Lambda X^2)/2}\,dX$ over its Gaussian part. So $F$ equals the logarithm of this integral in the Miwa variables $t_k = -(2k-1)!!\,\mathrm{tr}\,\Lambda^{-2k-1}$.

steps.slogan: Evaluate the matrix integral as a ratio of determinants of Airy functions.
steps.detail: The Harish-Chandra-Itzykson-Zuber formula for the unitary group turns the matrix integral into $\det(\text{Airy-type functions at } \lambda_i)/\Delta(\lambda)$, where $\Delta$ is the Vandermonde determinant.

steps.slogan: Show that this determinant ratio is a KdV [tau function](c:tau-function).
steps.detail: A ratio of determinants of Airy functions at the points $\lambda_i$ is the tau function of a point of the Sato Grassmannian in the Miwa variables. Such a function satisfies the [KdV hierarchy](c:kdv-hierarchy).

steps.slogan: Conclude that $e^{F}$ solves KdV with the normalization of the string equation.
steps.detail: Steps 2 to 5 identify $e^F$ with the matrix Airy tau function, so $U = \partial_0^2 F$ solves the KdV equation. The initial data of the string equation fix this solution among all KdV solutions.

concepts.c:intersection-number: The numbers $\langle\tau_d\rangle_g$ are the coefficients of the generating function.
concepts.c:moduli-space-of-curves: The $\psi$-classes live on the compactified moduli space and are integrated there.
concepts.c:tau-function: KdV solutions come from tau functions; the proof identifies this one.
concepts.c:kdv-hierarchy: The generating function satisfies these equations, which is the claim.
concepts.c:ribbon-graph: Metric ribbon graphs give a combinatorial model of the moduli space.

source.ref: M. Kontsevich, Intersection theory on the moduli space of curves and the matrix Airy function, Communications in Mathematical Physics 147 (1992), 1-23
source.note: Kontsevich proves the conjecture by the ribbon graph sum and the matrix Airy integral; the steps outline his sections.

statement: Let $f\colon X \to Y$ be a projective morphism of regular arithmetic varieties, smooth over $\mathbb Q$, with a [Kähler](c:kahler-manifold) fibre metric. Let $\bar E$ be a hermitian [vector bundle](c:vector-bundle) on $X$. In the rational [arithmetic Chow group](c:arithmetic-chow-group) of $Y$, $\widehat{\mathrm{ch}}(f_*\bar E) - a(T) = f_*\big(\widehat{\mathrm{ch}}(\bar E)\,\widehat{\mathrm{Td}}(Tf)\,(1 - a(R(Tf_{\mathbb C})))\big)$, where $T$ is the analytic torsion form.

hypotheses.text: $f\colon X \to Y$ is projective, $X$ and $Y$ are regular arithmetic varieties, and $f$ is smooth over $\mathbb Q$.
The relative tangent bundle $Tf$ carries a hermitian metric that is [Kähler](c:kahler-manifold) on the fibres.
$\bar E$ is a hermitian [vector bundle](c:vector-bundle) on $X$.

conclusion: The two sides agree in the rational [arithmetic Chow group](c:arithmetic-chow-group) of $Y$.

proofs.name: Factorization and torsion forms
proofs.slogan: Factor the morphism through projective space, correct the direct image by the Bismut-Koehler torsion form, and check closed immersions and projective space separately.
proofs.scope: The arithmetic Riemann-Roch theorem of Gillet-Soulé in all degrees; Arakelov theory is a theory, and this theorem is its main member. The proof is an outline of the cited paper.

roles.why: Projectivity gives the factorization through projective space used to split the proof.
The [Kähler](c:kahler-manifold) fibre metric defines the torsion form and the Laplacians on the fibres.
The metric on the [vector bundle](c:vector-bundle) defines the $L^2$ metric of the direct image and the Chern character.

steps.slogan: Factor $f$ into a closed immersion followed by a projective bundle projection.
steps.detail: Choose an embedding $X \hookrightarrow \mathbb P^N_Y$ over $Y$. Both sides of the formula are compatible with composition, up to Bott-Chern secondary classes. So it is enough to prove the formula for closed immersions and for the projection $\mathbb P^N_Y \to Y$.

steps.slogan: Attach the Bismut-Koehler analytic torsion form to the direct image.
steps.detail: The torsion form $T$ is a smooth form on $Y(\mathbb C)$. Its $\partial\bar\partial$ equals the difference between the Chern form of the $L^2$-metrized direct image and the integral of the Riemann-Roch integrand. So $\widehat{\mathrm{ch}}(f_*\bar E) - a(T)$ is a well defined arithmetic class.

steps.slogan: Prove the formula for closed immersions by deformation to the normal cone.
steps.detail: Deform the immersion to the zero section of its normal bundle, where the formula is a Koszul complex computation. Bismut's immersion theorem for torsion forms controls the metrics along the deformation. The $R$-genus enters through this comparison.

steps.slogan: Prove the formula for the projection of a projective bundle.
steps.detail: For $\mathbb P^N_Y \to Y$ the direct images of $\mathcal O(k)$ are explicit. The cited work compares their torsion forms, for the Fubini-Study metric, with the characteristic class side, where the $R$-genus appears.

steps.slogan: Assemble the two cases into the formula for $f$.
steps.detail: Steps 3 and 4 give the formula for both factors of $f$, and step 2 shows compatibility with composition. On the generic fibre the formula is the classical Grothendieck-Riemann-Roch theorem, so the arithmetic version refines it by Green forms.

concepts.c:kahler-manifold: The Kähler fibre metric makes the Laplacians and the torsion form defined.
concepts.c:vector-bundle: The hermitian bundle has a Chern character and an $L^2$ direct image.
concepts.c:arithmetic-chow-group: The identity holds in this group, which carries the Green form data.

source.ref: H. Gillet, D. Rössler and C. Soulé, An arithmetic Riemann-Roch theorem in higher degrees, Annales de l'Institut Fourier 58 (2008), 2169-2189
source.note: The degree one case is Gillet-Soulé, Inventiones Mathematicae 110 (1992), 473-543; the cited paper proves all degrees with Bismut-Koehler torsion forms.

statement: Every [real number](c:real-number) $x$ is smaller than some [natural number](c:natural-number) $n$.

hypotheses.text: Every nonempty subset of $\mathbb R$ that is bounded above has a [least upper bound](c:least-upper-bound).

proofs.name: Supremum of the naturals
proofs.slogan: If the naturals were bounded above, their supremum minus one would be a smaller upper bound, which is absurd.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem for $\mathbb R$. In other ordered structures, such as non-standard fields, the property can fail, so the completeness axiom is needed.

roles.why: The real number $x$ is the candidate upper bound that the proof tests.
Completeness gives a least upper bound for $\mathbb N$.

steps.slogan: Assume that $x$ is an upper bound of $\mathbb N$.
steps.detail: Suppose that no [natural number](c:natural-number) exceeds $x$. Then $\mathbb N \subset \mathbb R$ is nonempty (it contains 0) and bounded above by $x$.

steps.slogan: Take the [least upper bound](c:least-upper-bound) $s$ of $\mathbb N$.
steps.detail: By the completeness of the real numbers, the nonempty bounded set $\mathbb N$ has a least upper bound $s \in \mathbb R$.

steps.slogan: Find a natural number $n$ larger than $s-1$.
steps.detail: The number $s - 1$ is smaller than $s$, so it is not an upper bound of $\mathbb N$. Hence some $n \in \mathbb N$ satisfies $n > s - 1$.

steps.slogan: Add one to $n$ to exceed $s$ and reach a contradiction.
steps.detail: Since $n + 1 \in \mathbb N$ and $n + 1 > s$, the number $s$ is not an upper bound of $\mathbb N$. This contradicts the choice of $s$, so the assumption fails and some natural number exceeds $x$.

concepts.c:real-number: The statement and the completeness axiom concern the real numbers.
concepts.c:natural-number: The naturals form the set whose supremum leads to the contradiction.
concepts.c:least-upper-bound: The supremum of $\mathbb N$ is the object that the proof shifts by one.

source.note: Standard textbook proof from the least upper bound property.

statement: Let $r \ge 0$ be an integer and $0 < \alpha < 1$. Let $f$ be a continuous $2\pi$-[periodic](c:periodic-function) function whose [best approximation](c:best-approximation) error by [trigonometric polynomials](c:trigonometric-polynomial) of degree at most $n$ is $E_n(f) \le C n^{-(r+\alpha)}$ for all $n \ge 1$. Then $f \in C^r$ and the [modulus of continuity](c:modulus-of-continuity) of $f^{(r)}$ is $O(\delta^\alpha)$.

hypotheses.text: The uniform [best approximation](c:best-approximation) error satisfies $E_n(f) \le C n^{-(r+\alpha)}$ for every $n \ge 1$.
The integer $r \ge 0$ and the exponent $\alpha$ satisfy $0 < \alpha < 1$.

conclusion: The function $f$ has $r$ continuous derivatives, and $|f^{(r)}(x) - f^{(r)}(y)| \le C' |x-y|^\alpha$ for all $x, y$.

proofs.name: Telescoping with Bernstein's inequality
proofs.slogan: Write $f$ as a telescoping series of trigonometric polynomials of dyadic degree and bound their derivatives by Bernstein's inequality.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem for $0 < \alpha < 1$. For $\alpha = 1$ the same argument gives only the Zygmund class, not $C^{r,1}$.

roles.why: Periodicity and continuity make the best approximants exist in the sup norm.
The decay rate of $E_n(f)$ bounds every dyadic difference.
The condition $r + \alpha - j > 0$ makes the derivative series converge, and $\alpha < 1$ makes the sum over small scales converge.

steps.slogan: Choose best approximants $T_n$ and form the dyadic differences.
steps.detail: Let $T_n$ be a [trigonometric polynomial](c:trigonometric-polynomial) of degree at most $n$ with $\|f - T_n\|_\infty = E_n(f)$. It exists because the space is finite dimensional. Put $g_k = T_{2^{k+1}} - T_{2^k}$. Then $\|g_k\|_\infty \le 2C\, 2^{-k(r+\alpha)}$.

steps.slogan: Write $f$ as a uniformly convergent telescoping series.
steps.detail: Since $E_n(f) \to 0$, the polynomials $T_{2^k}$ converge uniformly to $f$. So $f = T_1 + \sum_{k \ge 0} g_k$ with uniform convergence.

steps.slogan: Bound the derivatives of each difference by Bernstein's inequality.
steps.detail: Bernstein's inequality says $\|T^{(j)}\|_\infty \le N^j \|T\|_\infty$ for a trigonometric polynomial $T$ of degree at most $N$. The polynomial $g_k$ has degree at most $2^{k+1}$, so $\|g_k^{(j)}\|_\infty \le 2^{j+1} C\, 2^{-k(r+\alpha-j)}$.

steps.slogan: Differentiate the series term by term up to order $r$.
steps.detail: For $j \le r$ the exponent $r + \alpha - j$ is positive, so $\sum_k \|g_k^{(j)}\|_\infty$ is finite. Hence the series of $j$-th derivatives converges uniformly, $f \in C^r$ and $f^{(r)} = T_1^{(r)} + \sum_k g_k^{(r)}$.

steps.slogan: Split the Hölder quotient of $f^{(r)}$ at the scale of the increment.
steps.detail: Let $0 < |h| \le 1$ and choose $K$ with $2^{-K-1} < |h| \le 2^{-K}$. For $k \le K$, use $\|g_k^{(r+1)}\| \le A\, 2^{k(1-\alpha)}$ and the mean value inequality. For $k > K$, use $2\|g_k^{(r)}\| \le A\, 2^{-k\alpha}$. Both sums are at most $c\,|h|^\alpha$ since $0 < \alpha < 1$.

concepts.c:periodic-function: Periodicity gives the sup norm over a circle and trigonometric approximants.
concepts.c:best-approximation: The errors $E_n(f)$ give the sizes of the dyadic differences.
concepts.c:trigonometric-polynomial: The approximants have bounded degree, so Bernstein's inequality applies.
concepts.c:modulus-of-continuity: The Hölder bound is a bound on the modulus of continuity of $f^{(r)}$.

source.note: Standard proof of the converse to Jackson's theorem; see Lorentz, Approximation of Functions, or DeVore and Lorentz, Constructive Approximation.

statement: Let $U \subset \mathbb R^2$ be a [simply connected](c:simply-connected-space) open set. Let $g$ be a smooth positive definite form, the candidate [first fundamental form](c:first-fundamental-form), and $h$ a smooth symmetric form, the candidate [second fundamental form](c:second-fundamental-form). Suppose that $g, h$ satisfy the Gauss and Codazzi-Mainardi equations. Then some [immersion](c:immersion) $F\colon U \to \mathbb R^3$ has these forms, and any two such immersions differ by a rotation and a translation.

hypotheses.text: $g$ is a smooth positive definite form and $h$ is a smooth symmetric form on $U$.
The pair $(g, h)$ satisfies the Gauss equation and the Codazzi-Mainardi equations.

conclusion: There is an [immersion](c:immersion) $F\colon U \to \mathbb R^3$ with first form $g$ and second form $h$ for its unit normal. It is unique up to a rotation and a translation of $\mathbb R^3$.

proofs.name: Moving frame and Frobenius
proofs.slogan: Write the structure equations as a linear system for the moving frame, solve it with the Frobenius theorem, and integrate the frame to the surface.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem for surfaces in $\mathbb R^3$ with a fixed unit normal. A reflection of $\mathbb R^3$ changes the sign of $h$, so uniqueness holds up to orientation preserving motions.

roles.why: Simple connectivity lets the Frobenius solution and the closed form integrate globally on $U$.
The forms $g$ and $h$ define the coefficient matrices $A_i$ and the initial Gram matrix.
The Gauss and Codazzi equations are the integrability conditions of the frame system.

steps.slogan: Write the Gauss-Weingarten equations as a linear system for a moving frame.
steps.detail: Put $\Phi = (F_1, F_2, N)$ with $F_i = \partial_i F$. The Gauss and Weingarten formulas $\partial_j F_i = \Gamma_{ij}^k F_k + h_{ij} N$ and $\partial_i N = -h_i^{\,k} F_k$ read $\partial_i \Phi = \Phi A_i$. The matrices $A_i$ depend only on $g$ and $h$, through the Christoffel symbols and the shape operator.

steps.slogan: Check that the integrability condition of the system is the Gauss and Codazzi equations.
steps.detail: The system is integrable exactly when $\partial_2 A_1 - \partial_1 A_2 = A_1 A_2 - A_2 A_1$. The tangent block of this identity is the Gauss equation, which says $\det h/\det g$ equals the curvature of $g$. The mixed blocks are the Codazzi-Mainardi equations.

steps.slogan: Solve the system on $U$ for an initial frame with the right Gram matrix.
steps.detail: Fix $p_0 \in U$ and $\Phi_0$ with $\Phi_0^T \Phi_0 = \mathrm{diag}(g(p_0), 1)$ and $\det \Phi_0 > 0$. The Frobenius theorem gives a global solution $\Phi$ on $U$. Both $\Phi^T\Phi$ and $\mathrm{diag}(g, 1)$ solve one linear system with equal initial values, so $\Phi^T\Phi = \mathrm{diag}(g, 1)$.

steps.slogan: Integrate the first two columns to obtain the surface $F$.
steps.detail: Because $\partial_j F_i$ is symmetric in $i, j$, the form $F_1\,du^1 + F_2\,du^2$ is closed. It has a primitive $F$ on the simply connected set $U$. Then $F_i \cdot F_j = g_{ij}$, so $F$ is an immersion with unit normal $N$, and $\partial_j F_i \cdot N = h_{ij}$.

steps.slogan: Match the frames of two solutions at one point by a rotation.
steps.detail: Let $\tilde F$ have the same forms. At $p_0$ the frames satisfy $\tilde\Phi_0 = R\Phi_0$ for some $R \in SO(3)$. Both $R\Phi$ and $\tilde\Phi$ solve the linear system with equal values at $p_0$, so they agree on $U$ by uniqueness of linear ODE solutions along paths. Then $d(\tilde F - RF) = 0$, so $\tilde F = RF + c$.

concepts.c:simply-connected-space: Simple connectivity makes closed forms and Frobenius solutions global.
concepts.c:first-fundamental-form: The form $g$ fixes the lengths and the Gram matrix of the frame.
concepts.c:second-fundamental-form: The form $h$ fixes how the normal turns along the surface.
concepts.c:immersion: The integrated map has independent partial derivatives, so it is an immersion.

source.note: Standard proof by the moving frame method; see do Carmo, Differential Geometry of Curves and Surfaces, or Spivak, A Comprehensive Introduction to Differential Geometry, vol. 3.

statement: Let $X$ be a [Stein manifold](c:stein-manifold) and $\mathcal F$ a [coherent](c:coherent-sheaf) analytic sheaf on $X$. Theorem A: for every $x \in X$ the stalk $\mathcal F_x$ is generated over $\mathcal O_{X,x}$ by global sections of $\mathcal F$. Theorem B: the [sheaf cohomology](c:sheaf-cohomology) groups $H^q(X, \mathcal F)$ vanish for all $q \ge 1$.

hypotheses.text: $\mathcal F$ is a [coherent](c:coherent-sheaf) analytic sheaf on $X$.

conclusion: Global sections generate every stalk of $\mathcal F$, and $H^q(X, \mathcal F) = 0$ for $q \ge 1$.

proofs.name: Cartan's matrix lemma and exhaustion
proofs.slogan: Prove vanishing of higher cohomology over polyhedra by Cartan's matrix lemma, pass to the Stein manifold by exhaustion, and get generation by Nakayama's lemma.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, for any coherent analytic sheaf on any Stein manifold. The proof is an outline of Cartan's argument; Theorem B is the main step and Theorem A follows from it.

roles.why: The Stein property gives the exhaustion by analytic polyhedra, each Runge in the next.
Coherence gives local finite presentations and makes $\mathfrak m_x\mathcal F$ coherent.

steps.slogan: Use Oka's coherence theorem to give $\mathcal F$ local finite free presentations.
steps.detail: By Oka's theorem the structure sheaf $\mathcal O_X$ is coherent, so kernels of maps $\mathcal O^p \to \mathcal O^q$ are finitely generated. A [coherent](c:coherent-sheaf) sheaf $\mathcal F$ therefore has, near each point, a finite resolution by free sheaves $\mathcal O^p$.

steps.slogan: Prove vanishing of higher cohomology over compact polyhedra by Cartan's matrix lemma.
steps.detail: Cartan's lemma factors an invertible holomorphic matrix close to the identity on the intersection of two compact boxes into matrices holomorphic on each box. With it, Cousin-type problems are solved first for $\mathcal O^p$ and then for $\mathcal F$ near compact polydiscs and analytic polyhedra.

steps.slogan: Exhaust the Stein manifold by polyhedra and pass to the limit.
steps.detail: A [Stein manifold](c:stein-manifold) is an increasing union of relatively compact analytic polyhedra, each Runge in the next. Approximation of sections between steps and a Mittag-Leffler argument in Fréchet spaces give $H^q(X, \mathcal F) = 0$ for $q \ge 1$. This is Theorem B.

steps.slogan: Derive Theorem A from Theorem B at each point by Nakayama's lemma.
steps.detail: Let $\mathfrak m_x$ be the ideal sheaf of $x$. In $0 \to \mathfrak m_x\mathcal F \to \mathcal F \to \mathcal F/\mathfrak m_x\mathcal F \to 0$ the sheaf $\mathfrak m_x\mathcal F$ is coherent, so $H^1(X, \mathfrak m_x\mathcal F) = 0$. Global sections then span $\mathcal F_x/\mathfrak m_x\mathcal F_x$, and Nakayama's lemma gives generation of the finitely generated module $\mathcal F_x$. With step 3 this proves A and B.

concepts.c:stein-manifold: Stein manifolds are exhausted by polyhedra where the vanishing is first proved.
concepts.c:coherent-sheaf: Coherence gives local finite presentations and control of kernels.
concepts.c:sheaf-cohomology: Theorem B states the vanishing of these groups.

source.ref: H. Cartan, Variétés analytiques complexes et cohomologie, in Colloque sur les fonctions de plusieurs variables, Bruxelles 1953, Georges Thone and Masson, 1953, pp. 41-55
source.note: Cartan states and proves Theorems A and B there, after the Cartan seminars of 1951-52; the steps outline that argument.

statement: Let $S$ be a scheme and $G$ a commutative [finite flat group scheme](c:finite-flat-group-scheme) over $S$. The functor $G^D = \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}(G, \mathbb G_m)$ is a commutative finite flat group scheme, namely the spectrum of the dual [Hopf algebra](c:hopf-algebra) of $\mathcal O_G$. The natural map $G \to (G^D)^D$ is an isomorphism.

hypotheses.text: $G$ is a [finite flat group scheme](c:finite-flat-group-scheme) over $S$: its coordinate ring is a locally free module of finite rank.

conclusion: The Cartier dual $G^D$ is represented by $\mathrm{Spec}$ of the dual Hopf algebra, and $G \to (G^D)^D$ is an isomorphism.

proofs.name: Dual Hopf algebra
proofs.slogan: Identify characters of $G$ with group-like elements, match them with algebra maps from the dual Hopf algebra, and check that dualizing twice is the identity.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem for finite locally free commutative group schemes over any base. The constant group of a finite abelian group is dual to the diagonalizable group of its [Pontryagin dual](c:pontryagin-dual); this is the sense in which Cartier duality refines Pontryagin duality.

roles.why: Finite projectivity makes $A^\vee \otimes A^\vee = (A \otimes A)^\vee$ and $A^{\vee\vee} = A$.
Commutativity of $G$ makes $A$ cocommutative, so $A^\vee$ is a commutative algebra.

steps.slogan: Reduce to an affine base $S = \mathrm{Spec}\,R$ with $G = \mathrm{Spec}\,A$.
steps.detail: Both $G^D$ and the dual algebra commute with base change, and an isomorphism of sheaves can be checked locally on $S$. Locally $A = \mathcal O_G$ is a finite projective $R$-module with the Hopf algebra structure of the [group scheme](c:group-scheme) $G$.

steps.slogan: Give the dual module $A^\vee = \mathrm{Hom}_R(A, R)$ a Hopf algebra structure.
steps.detail: Since $A$ is finite projective, $(A \otimes A)^\vee = A^\vee \otimes A^\vee$. Transposing comultiplication, multiplication, counit, unit and antipode gives multiplication, comultiplication, unit, counit and antipode of $A^\vee$. Cocommutativity of $A$ makes $A^\vee$ a commutative [Hopf algebra](c:hopf-algebra).

steps.slogan: Identify characters of $G$ over an algebra $R'$ with group-like elements of $A \otimes R'$.
steps.detail: A homomorphism $G_{R'} \to \mathbb G_{m,R'}$ is a unit $u \in A \otimes R'$ with $\Delta(u) = u \otimes u$. Applying the counit gives $\epsilon(u)u = u$, so $\epsilon(u) = 1$ since $u$ is a unit.

steps.slogan: Match group-like elements with algebra maps from $A^\vee$.
steps.detail: Since $A \otimes R' = \mathrm{Hom}_{R'}(A^\vee \otimes R', R')$, an element $u$ gives a linear map $\hat u$. The identity $\Delta(u) = u \otimes u$ says that $\hat u$ is multiplicative, and $\epsilon(u) = 1$ says $\hat u(1) = 1$. So $G^D(R') = \mathrm{Hom}_{R'\text{-alg}}(A^\vee \otimes R', R')$, the points of $\mathrm{Spec}\,A^\vee$. Multiplying characters is the coproduct of $A^\vee$.

steps.slogan: Check that dualizing twice returns the original Hopf algebra.
steps.detail: For a finite projective module the evaluation map $A \to (A^\vee)^\vee$ is an isomorphism, and it commutes with all Hopf algebra maps because transposing twice is the identity. It induces $G \to (G^D)^D$, which sends a point $g$ to the character $\chi \mapsto \chi(g)$. So this map is an isomorphism.

concepts.c:finite-flat-group-scheme: Finite flatness makes the coordinate ring a finite projective module with a dual.
concepts.c:hopf-algebra: The dual of the coordinate ring is again a Hopf algebra.
concepts.c:group-scheme: The group scheme structure is encoded by the Hopf algebra of its coordinate ring.
concepts.c:pontryagin-dual: Cartier duality extends the Pontryagin dual of finite abelian groups.

source.note: Standard proof by linear duality of the coordinate ring, as in the treatments of finite group schemes by Oort and Tate.

statement: Let $m, n > 1$ be [coprime integers](c:coprime-integers). Then $mn - m - n$ is not of the form $am + bn$ with [natural numbers](c:natural-number) $a, b$, and every natural number $k > mn - m - n$ is of that form.
conclusion: The number $mn - m - n$ is the largest [natural number](c:natural-number) that is not of the form $am + bn$ with $a, b \ge 0$.

proofs.name: Bézout and residues
proofs.slogan: Show by divisibility that the number $mn-m-n$ has no representation, and build a representation of every larger number from Bézout's identity.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem for $m, n > 1$. The case $m = 1$ or $n = 1$ is excluded: then every natural number is representable and there is no largest gap.

roles.why: Coprimality gives the divisibility step and Bézout's identity for $k$.
The bound $m > 1$ gives $m + n \le mn$, so no subtraction is truncated.
The bound $n > 1$ gives $m + n \le mn$ together with $m > 1$.

steps.slogan: Rewrite membership in the generated monoid as a representation $k = am + bn$.
steps.detail: The additive submonoid of $\mathbb N$ generated by $m$ and $n$ is the set of numbers $am + bn$ with $a, b \in \mathbb N$. So the claim is that $mn - m - n$ has no such representation and every larger number has one.

steps.slogan: Show that $mn - m - n$ has no representation $am + bn$.
steps.detail: Suppose $mn - m - n = am + bn$. Since $m + n \le mn$, this gives $(a+1)m + (b+1)n = mn$. Then $n \mid (a+1)m$, so $n \mid a + 1$ by coprimality, and $a + 1 \ge n$. Likewise $b + 1 \ge m$. The left side is at least $2mn > mn$, a contradiction.

steps.slogan: Solve $am + bn = k$ over the integers with Bézout's identity.
steps.detail: Because $\gcd(m, n) = 1$, Bézout's identity gives integers $x, y$ with $xm + yn = 1$. Multiplying by $k$ gives integers $a_0, b_0$ with $a_0 m + b_0 n = k$.

steps.slogan: Reduce the coefficient of $m$ modulo $n$ to the range $0$ to $n - 1$.
steps.detail: Write $a_0 = qn + a$ with $0 \le a \le n - 1$, and put $b = b_0 + qm$. Then $am + bn = k$ and $0 \le a \le n - 1$.

steps.slogan: Show that $b \ge 0$ whenever $k > mn - m - n$.
steps.detail: If $b \le -1$, then $k = am + bn \le (n-1)m - n = mn - m - n$, against $k > mn - m - n$. So $b \ge 0$ and $k = am + bn$ is a representation with natural numbers.

steps.slogan: Combine both halves to see that $mn - m - n$ is the greatest gap.
steps.detail: Step 2 shows that $mn - m - n$ is not representable. Step 5 shows that every larger [natural number](c:natural-number) is representable. So $mn - m - n$ is the largest natural number outside the monoid.

concepts.c:coprime-integers: Coprimality gives Bézout's identity and the divisibility step.
concepts.c:natural-number: Representations use natural number coefficients, and the greatest gap is a natural number.

source.note: mathlib uses AddSubmonoid.mem_closure_pair, Nat.Coprime.mul_add_mul_ne_mul for the gap, and Nat.exists_add_mul_eq_of_gcd_dvd_of_mul_pred_le (Bézout and reduction modulo $n$) for the larger numbers.

statement: Let $G$ be a finite [chordal graph](c:chordal-graph) that is not complete. Then $G$ has two nonadjacent [simplicial vertices](c:simplicial-vertex). Hence every finite chordal graph has a simplicial vertex.

hypotheses.text: $G$ is [chordal](c:chordal-graph): every cycle of length at least 4 has a chord.
$G$ is not complete: some two vertices are nonadjacent.

conclusion: Two nonadjacent vertices of $G$ have neighborhoods that are [cliques](c:clique), and every chordal graph has such a vertex.

proofs.name: Minimal separators are cliques
proofs.slogan: Take a minimal separator of two nonadjacent vertices, show that it is a clique, and find a simplicial vertex on each side by induction.
proofs.scope: Dirac's theorem. In a complete graph every vertex is simplicial, which gives the second sentence. Deleting a simplicial vertex keeps a chordal graph chordal, so repeating gives a perfect elimination ordering.

roles.why: Finiteness allows induction on the number of vertices and shortest paths.
Chords of the cycle built from two shortest paths force the separator to be a clique.
Two nonadjacent vertices exist to be separated.

steps.slogan: Pick nonadjacent vertices $u, v$ and a minimal set $S$ separating them.
steps.detail: Let $S$ be a set of vertices of least size whose removal puts $u$ and $v$ in different [connected components](c:connected-component) $A \ni u$ and $B \ni v$ of $G - S$. It exists since $V \setminus \{u, v\}$ separates them. Minimality gives every $s \in S$ a neighbor in $A$ and a neighbor in $B$.

steps.slogan: Show that the separator $S$ is a [clique](c:clique).
steps.detail: Take $s \ne t$ in $S$ nonadjacent. Choose a shortest $s$-$t$ path through $A$ and one through $B$. Together they form a cycle of length at least 4. A chord can join neither $A$ to $B$ nor two nonconsecutive vertices of one shortest path, so it is $st$, a contradiction.

steps.slogan: Apply induction to the [induced subgraph](c:induced-subgraph) on $A \cup S$.
steps.detail: The subgraph $G_A = G[A \cup S]$ is chordal and has fewer vertices than $G$, since it misses $B$. If it is complete, every vertex of $G_A$ is simplicial in it. Otherwise induction gives two nonadjacent simplicial vertices of $G_A$.

steps.slogan: Find a simplicial vertex of $G_A$ that lies in $A$.
steps.detail: The set $S$ is a clique, so it does not hold two nonadjacent vertices. Hence some simplicial vertex $a$ of $G_A$ lies in $A$. In the complete case any vertex of $A$ works, and $A \ne \emptyset$ because $u \in A$.

steps.slogan: Show that $a$ is simplicial in $G$ and repeat the argument on $B$.
steps.detail: Since $A$ is a component of $G - S$, all neighbors of $a$ lie in $A \cup S$, so its neighborhood in $G$ equals that in $G_A$, a clique. The same argument gives a simplicial $b \in B$. Vertices of different components are nonadjacent, so $a$ and $b$ are nonadjacent.

concepts.c:graph: The theorem concerns finite simple graphs.
concepts.c:chordal-graph: Chords of long cycles are the only property of the graph used.
concepts.c:simplicial-vertex: The proof constructs two such vertices.
concepts.c:clique: A clique separator keeps a simplicial vertex of a side simplicial in $G$.
concepts.c:connected-component: The sides $A$ and $B$ are components of $G - S$.
concepts.c:induced-subgraph: Induction runs on the chordal induced subgraph $G[A \cup S]$.

source.note: Dirac's proof (G. A. Dirac, On rigid circuit graphs, Abhandlungen aus dem Mathematischen Seminar der Universität Hamburg 25 (1961), 71-76).

new_concepts.name: chordal graph
new_concepts.reminder: A graph in which every cycle of length at least four has a chord.
new_concepts.definition: A graph is chordal if every cycle of length at least 4 has a chord, an edge that joins two nonconsecutive vertices of the cycle.

new_concepts.name: simplicial vertex
new_concepts.reminder: A vertex of a graph whose neighbors are pairwise adjacent.
new_concepts.definition: A vertex of a graph is simplicial if its neighbors form a clique, so the vertex lies in exactly one maximal clique.

statement: Let $M$ be a [paracompact Hausdorff](c:paracompact-hausdorff-space) topological [manifold with boundary](c:manifold-with-boundary). Then $\partial M$ has a collar: an [open neighbourhood](c:open-neighbourhood) $U$ of $\partial M$ in $M$ and a [homeomorphism](c:homeomorphism) $U \to \partial M \times [0,1)$ that sends each $x \in \partial M$ to $(x, 0)$.
conclusion: There are an [open neighbourhood](c:open-neighbourhood) $U \supseteq \partial M$ and a [homeomorphism](c:homeomorphism) $U \cong \partial M \times [0,1)$ that is the identity on $\partial M \times \{0\}$.

proofs.name: Pushing in an external collar
proofs.slogan: Collar the boundary locally, attach an external collar, and push the new boundary into the manifold through the local collars one at a time.
proofs.scope: The topological collar theorem of Brown, for every paracompact Hausdorff manifold with boundary. In the smooth case a collar also comes from the flow of an inward vector field. The proof is an outline of Connelly's argument.

roles.why: Half-space charts give the local collars near boundary points.
Paracompactness gives a locally finite cover and a partition of unity, so infinitely many pushes compose.

steps.slogan: Collar the boundary locally with half-space charts.
steps.detail: A chart near $x \in \partial M$ maps to $\mathbb R^{n-1} \times [0, \infty)$ with boundary points going to $\mathbb R^{n-1} \times \{0\}$. Pulling back the translation in the last coordinate gives an open embedding $W \times [0,1) \to M$, the identity on $W \times \{0\}$, for a neighborhood $W$ of $x$ in $\partial M$.

steps.slogan: Cover the boundary by a locally finite family with local collars.
steps.detail: The boundary is closed in the paracompact space $M$, so it is paracompact. The sets $W$ have a locally finite refinement $\{W_i\}$ with local collars $c_i$, and a subordinate [partition of unity](c:partition-of-unity) $\{\phi_i\}$ on $\partial M$.

steps.slogan: Attach an external collar to enlarge $M$ to a space $M'$.
steps.detail: Let $M' = M \cup_{\partial M} (\partial M \times [-1, 0])$, a manifold with boundary $\partial M \times \{-1\}$. The aim is a homeomorphism $h \colon M' \to M$. Then $h$ maps the open set $\partial M \times [-1, 0)$ onto an open neighbourhood of $\partial M$ in $M$, and this is the collar after reparametrization.

steps.slogan: Push the boundary inward through one local collar at a time.
steps.detail: For each index $i$, build a homeomorphism $h_i$ of the enlarged space supported in the image of the local collar $c_i$. It moves boundary points over $W_i$ inward by an amount controlled by $\phi_i$. The pushes are built in the order of the index, so that each one respects the earlier ones.

steps.slogan: Compose the pushes into a homeomorphism from $M'$ onto $M$.
steps.detail: The supports are locally finite, so the infinite composite $h$ is a well defined homeomorphism. After all pushes the boundary lies in $M$ and $h(M') = M$. The image $h(\partial M \times [-1, 0))$ is open in $M$, contains $\partial M$, and is homeomorphic to $\partial M \times [0, 1)$.

concepts.c:paracompact-hausdorff-space: Paracompactness gives locally finite covers and partitions of unity for the pushes.
concepts.c:manifold-with-boundary: Boundary charts to the half-space give the local collars.
concepts.c:open-neighbourhood: The collar is an open neighbourhood of the boundary.
concepts.c:homeomorphism: The collar is a homeomorphism, built as a composite of homeomorphisms.
concepts.c:partition-of-unity: The partition of unity controls how far each push moves points.

source.ref: R. Connelly, A new proof of Brown's collaring theorem, Proceedings of the American Mathematical Society 27 (1971), 180-182
source.note: Connelly adds a collar to the space and builds a homeomorphism by pushing one collared open set at a time; Brown's original proof is Annals of Mathematics 75 (1962), 331-341.

statement: The set of [rational numbers](c:rational-number) is [countable](c:countable-set) and infinite: some [bijection](c:bijection) maps $\mathbb N$ onto $\mathbb Q$.
conclusion: There is a bijection $\mathbb N \to \mathbb Q$.

proofs.name: Pairing function
proofs.slogan: Send each rational in lowest terms to a pair of natural numbers, code the pair by one natural number, and list the used numbers in order.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. The set $\mathbb Q$ is infinite, so the result is a bijection with $\mathbb N$, not only an injection.

steps.slogan: Write each rational uniquely as $p/q$ in lowest terms with $q \ge 1$.
steps.detail: Divide numerator and denominator of a fraction by their greatest common divisor to get $p/q$ with $q \ge 1$ and $\gcd(p, q) = 1$. Two such fractions are equal only if their pairs $(p, q)$ are equal, by cross multiplication and coprimality. So $x \mapsto (p, q)$ is injective from $\mathbb Q$ to $\mathbb Z \times \mathbb Z_{\ge 1}$.

steps.slogan: Map the integers into the natural numbers one to one.
steps.detail: Send $z \ge 0$ to $2z$ and $z < 0$ to $-2z - 1$. This map $\mathbb Z \to \mathbb N$ is a bijection. With the shift $q \mapsto q - 1$ it embeds $\mathbb Z \times \mathbb Z_{\ge 1}$ into $\mathbb N \times \mathbb N$ injectively.

steps.slogan: Code two natural numbers by one with the Cantor [pairing function](c:pairing-function).
steps.detail: Put $\pi(a, b) = \tfrac{(a+b)(a+b+1)}{2} + b$. If $a + b = d$, then $\pi(a,b)$ lies in $[\tfrac{d(d+1)}{2}, \tfrac{(d+1)(d+2)}{2})$, and these intervals are disjoint. Inside one interval, $\pi$ determines $b$. So $\pi$ is injective, and the composite gives an injection $\iota \colon \mathbb Q \to \mathbb N$.

steps.slogan: List the image of $\iota$ in increasing order.
steps.detail: The image $I = \iota(\mathbb Q)$ is infinite, because the distinct integers $n = n/1$ have distinct images. Listing $I$ in increasing order gives a bijection $\mathbb N \to I$. Composing with $\iota^{-1} \colon I \to \mathbb Q$ gives a bijection $\mathbb N \to \mathbb Q$.

concepts.c:rational-number: The proof codes each rational by its reduced fraction.
concepts.c:countable-set: The theorem says that the rationals form a countable set.
concepts.c:bijection: The final map from the natural numbers is a bijection.
concepts.c:pairing-function: The pairing function codes two natural numbers as one.

source.note: Standard argument with the Cantor pairing function (item 3 of Freek Wiedijk's list of 100 theorems).

statement: Let $\psi\colon \mathbb N \to [0, \infty)$ be nonincreasing. Let $W(\psi)$ be the set of real $x$ with $|qx - p| < \psi(q)$ for infinitely many integer pairs $(p, q)$ with $q \ge 1$. If $\sum_q \psi(q) < \infty$, then $W(\psi)$ is a [null set](c:null-set). If $\sum_q \psi(q) = \infty$, then [almost every](c:almost-everywhere) real number lies in $W(\psi)$.

hypotheses.text: $\psi$ takes values in $[0, \infty)$ and is nonincreasing.

conclusion: The set $W(\psi)$ has measure 0 when $\sum \psi(q)$ converges and full measure when it diverges.

proofs.name: Borel-Cantelli and overlap estimates
proofs.slogan: Use the Borel-Cantelli lemma for the convergent case, and for the divergent case bound the overlaps of the reduced sets, get positive measure, and apply a zero-one law.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem (Khinchin's theorem). The convergent part needs no monotonicity; the divergent part fails without it, by the Duffin-Schaeffer counterexample. The proof is an outline of the measure-theoretic proof.

roles.why: Monotonicity gives the divergence of the reduced series and the overlap estimate.

steps.slogan: Describe $W(\psi)$ as a limsup set of intervals around fractions.
steps.detail: For $q \ge 1$ let $A_q = \{x \in [0,1] : |qx - p| < \psi(q) \text{ for some } p\}$. Then $\mu(A_q) \le 2\psi(q)$ for the [Lebesgue measure](c:lebesgue-measure) $\mu$. For fixed $q$ only finitely many $p$ qualify, so $x \in W(\psi)$ means that $x$ lies in infinitely many $A_q$, up to integer translation.

steps.slogan: Apply the Borel-Cantelli lemma when the series converges.
steps.detail: If $\sum \psi(q) < \infty$, then $\sum \mu(A_q) \le 2\sum \psi(q) < \infty$. The Borel-Cantelli lemma gives $\mu(\limsup A_q) = 0$. By periodicity, $W(\psi)$ is a null set.

steps.slogan: Pass to the sets of reduced fractions when the series diverges.
steps.detail: Replace $\psi$ by $\min(\psi, 1/2)$, which keeps divergence. Let $A_q^*$ keep the $x$ within $\psi(q)/q$ of a fraction $p/q$ with $\gcd(p, q) = 1$. Since $\psi$ is nonincreasing, dyadic blocks give $\sum \varphi(q)\psi(q)/q = \infty$, with $\varphi$ Euler's function. So $\sum \mu(A_q^*) = \infty$.

steps.slogan: Bound the overlaps of the reduced sets on average.
steps.detail: Duffin and Schaeffer count the pairs of reduced fractions $p/q$ and $p'/r$ that lie close together. For monotone $\psi$ this gives $\sum_{q,r \le N} \mu(A_q^* \cap A_r^*) \le C\big(\sum_{q \le N} \mu(A_q^*)\big)^2$ for infinitely many $N$, with $C$ independent of $N$.

steps.slogan: Obtain positive measure for the limsup set from the Chung-Erdős inequality.
steps.detail: The Chung-Erdős (Kochen-Stone) inequality turns the overlap bound and the divergence of $\sum \mu(A_q^*)$ into $\mu(\limsup A_q^*) \ge 1/C > 0$.

steps.slogan: Upgrade positive measure to full measure by a zero-one law.
steps.detail: A zero-one law of Cassels and Gallagher shows that $\limsup A_q^*$ has measure 0 or 1. Step 5 excludes 0, so it has full measure. Since $\limsup A_q^* \subseteq W(\psi)$ up to translation, $W(\psi)$ has full measure.

steps.slogan: Combine the convergent and the divergent case.
steps.detail: Step 2 gives measure zero when the series converges. Step 6 gives full measure when it diverges. These two cases cover every nonincreasing $\psi$.

concepts.c:null-set: The convergent case concludes that $W(\psi)$ is a null set.
concepts.c:almost-everywhere: The divergent case concludes that almost every real lies in $W(\psi)$.
concepts.c:lebesgue-measure: The measures $\mu(A_q)$ drive the Borel-Cantelli and overlap arguments.

source.ref: G. Harman, Metric Number Theory, London Mathematical Society Monographs, New Series 18, Oxford University Press (Clarendon Press), 1998
source.note: The book proves Khinchin's theorem and the Duffin-Schaeffer theorem; the theorem is due to Khinchin, Mathematische Annalen 92 (1924), 115-125, by continued fractions.

statement: Let $E$ be a [holomorphic vector bundle](c:holomorphic-vector-bundle) over a compact [Kähler manifold](c:kahler-manifold) $(X, \omega)$. Then $E$ admits a [Hermitian-Einstein metric](c:hermitian-einstein-metric) if and only if $E$ is polystable, that is a direct sum of [slope-stable](c:slope-stability) bundles of the same slope.
conclusion: The bundle $E$ carries a Hermitian-Einstein metric exactly when $E$ is polystable.

proofs.name: Perturbed equation and weak limits
proofs.slogan: Show the easy direction by Chern-Weil theory, solve a perturbed equation for stable bundles, and show by weak limits that stability bounds the solutions.
proofs.scope: Both directions, for a holomorphic vector bundle on a compact Kähler manifold. Donaldson proved the projective algebraic case (1985, 1987); the proof here is an outline of Uhlenbeck and Yau's Kähler case.

roles.why: The Kähler form defines the contraction $\Lambda$, the degrees and the elliptic operator of the equation.
The bundle supplies subsheaves, degrees and the metrics $h$ on which the equation is posed.

steps.slogan: Show that a [Hermitian-Einstein metric](c:hermitian-einstein-metric) forces polystability by the degree formula.
steps.detail: For a coherent subsheaf $F \subset E$, the Chern-Weil formula and the sign of the second fundamental form give $\mu(F) \le \mu(E)$, with equality only when $F$ is a parallel direct summand. So $E$ is semistable and splits into stable summands of equal slope.

steps.slogan: Perturb the Hermitian-Einstein equation so that a solution exists for each $\varepsilon > 0$.
steps.detail: For stable $E$ and $\varepsilon \in (0, 1]$ solve $\sqrt{-1}\Lambda F_h - \lambda\,\mathrm{id} + \varepsilon \log(h_0^{-1} h) = 0$. It is solvable at $\varepsilon = 1$. The set of solvable $\varepsilon$ is open by ellipticity and closed by a $C^0$ estimate for fixed $\varepsilon$.

steps.slogan: Normalize an unbounded family of solutions to get a nonzero weak limit.
steps.detail: Suppose the solutions $h_\varepsilon$ are unbounded in $C^0$ as $\varepsilon \to 0$. Uhlenbeck and Yau show that the normalized logarithms $u_\varepsilon$ are bounded in $L^2_1$ and converge weakly to a nonzero $u_\infty$. A spectral projection $\pi$ of $u_\infty$ is a weakly holomorphic subbundle: $\pi \in L^2_1$ and $(1 - \pi)\bar\partial\pi = 0$.

steps.slogan: Turn the weak limit into a coherent subsheaf that contradicts stability.
steps.detail: By the Uhlenbeck-Yau regularity theorem, such a projection $\pi$ defines a coherent subsheaf, a subbundle off a set of codimension 2. A degree computation with the limit equation gives $\mu(F) \ge \mu(E)$, against [slope stability](c:slope-stability). So the solutions $h_\varepsilon$ stay bounded.

steps.slogan: Pass to the limit in the perturbed equation to get a Hermitian-Einstein metric.
steps.detail: A uniform $C^0$ bound gives $C^k$ bounds for all $k$ by elliptic estimates. By Arzelà-Ascoli a subsequence converges as $\varepsilon \to 0$ to a metric with $\sqrt{-1}\Lambda F_h = \lambda\,\mathrm{id}$. So every stable bundle has a Hermitian-Einstein metric.

steps.slogan: Treat a polystable bundle summand by summand and combine with the converse.
steps.detail: A polystable $E = \bigoplus E_i$ gets the direct sum of the metrics of the stable summands $E_i$, with equal constants $\lambda$ because the slopes agree. With step 1 this proves both directions.

concepts.c:hermitian-einstein-metric: Existence of this metric is the property that the theorem characterizes.
concepts.c:slope-stability: Stability is the condition that bounds the perturbed solutions.
concepts.c:kahler-manifold: The Kähler form defines the degrees and the elliptic operator.
concepts.c:holomorphic-vector-bundle: The bundle carries the metrics and subsheaves studied.

source.ref: K. Uhlenbeck and S.-T. Yau, On the existence of Hermitian-Yang-Mills connections in stable vector bundles, Communications on Pure and Applied Mathematics 39 (1986), S257-S293
source.note: Uhlenbeck and Yau prove the Kähler case; Donaldson, Proc. London Math. Soc. 50 (1985) and Duke Math. J. 54 (1987), proved the projective case.

statement: There is an absolute constant $c$ such that for every integer $k \ge 1$, every finite [graph](c:graph) has $k$ vertex-disjoint [cycles](c:cycle) or a [feedback vertex set](c:feedback-vertex-set) of at most $c\,k\log(k+1)$ vertices.
conclusion: Either $G$ has $k$ pairwise vertex-disjoint cycles, or some set of at most $c\,k\log(k+1)$ vertices meets every cycle of $G$.

proofs.name: Short cycles in reduced multigraphs
proofs.slogan: Reduce to minimum degree 3, use that such multigraphs have short cycles, and pack short cycles greedily to bound the feedback vertex set.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem (Erdős-Pósa), with the bound of order $k \log k$, which is best possible up to the constant. The proof is an outline of the cited paper, with the cubic case computed.

roles.why: The graph is reduced to a multigraph, and the final set is lifted back to it.
The number $k$ of disjoint cycles sets the length of the greedy packing and the size bound.

steps.slogan: Reduce $G$ to a multigraph of minimum degree at least 3.
steps.detail: Delete vertices of degree at most 1 and suppress vertices of degree 2, allowing loops and parallel edges. Cycles of the reduced multigraph $G_0$ correspond to cycles of $G$, disjoint families correspond, and a vertex set meeting all cycles of $G_0$ meets all cycles of $G$.

steps.slogan: Find a short cycle in a multigraph of minimum degree 3.
steps.detail: Grow a breadth-first tree from a vertex of a multigraph with $n$ vertices and minimum degree 3. If no cycle has at most $2\log_2 n + 3$ vertices, every vertex has two children down to depth $\log_2 n + 1$, which gives more than $n$ vertices. So a short cycle exists.

steps.slogan: Pack short cycles greedily in a cubic multigraph.
steps.detail: Let $H$ be 3-regular on $n$ vertices. Remove a shortest cycle with $\ell$ vertices and reduce again. The degree deficit is at most $\ell$, so at most $\ell$ more vertices vanish and the graph is cubic again. After $k$ rounds $k$ disjoint cycles exist once $n \ge c'k\log(k+1)$.

steps.slogan: Extend the bound to all multigraphs of minimum degree 3.
steps.detail: The cited paper proves that a multigraph with minimum degree 3 and no $k$ disjoint cycles has a set of at most $c\,k\log(k+1)$ vertices meeting every cycle, for an absolute constant $c$. The cubic computation of step 3 is the model case.

steps.slogan: Lift the vertex set from the reduced multigraph to $G$.
steps.detail: Apply step 4 to the reduced multigraph $G_0$ of step 1. Either $G_0$, hence $G$, has $k$ disjoint cycles, or the set found meets every cycle of $G_0$, hence every cycle of $G$.

concepts.c:graph: The theorem concerns finite graphs and their reduced multigraphs.
concepts.c:cycle: Disjoint cycles are the packing, and the feedback set meets all cycles.
concepts.c:feedback-vertex-set: The bound on this set is the conclusion.

source.ref: P. Erdős and L. Pósa, On independent circuits contained in a graph, Canadian Journal of Mathematics 17 (1965), 347-352
source.note: Erdős and Pósa prove the bounds c1 k log k < r(k) < c2 k log k; the steps outline the upper bound.
